| [THEORY-017](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-017.md) v4 | In a Hilbert-space model only unitarily invariant structure is intrinsic; a basis or tensor factorisation, and so any parts or features, is extra data supplied from outside the space, and the record's Hilbert-space works differ in where they get it | Carroll (2021), [LIT-123](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-123.md): a quantum theory is fixed up to unitary equivalence by the Hamiltonian's spectrum, and subsystems come from a factorisation that the dynamics must select. Van Rijsbergen ([LIT-262](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-262.md)) computes only traces and inner products, and treats each observable's eigenbasis as a "point of view". DisCoCat's ε/η composition ([LIT-273](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-273.md)) is orthogonally covariant, while its Frobenius sequel ([LIT-272](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-272.md)) stipulates a basis and composes by elementwise product in it. [THEORY-004](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-004.md) is the same point for learned representations. This is a synthesis across the four, not a result any one of them states. It does not say that basis-dependent models are wrong; it says what they have assumed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-261](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-261.md) v2 | In sparse distributed memory, recall of uniform random data from exact cues is a signal-to-noise problem whose optimum activates about (2MT)^-1/3 of the hard locations, and capacity then grows in proportion to the number of hard locations, rising toward about a tenth of them at 0.999 bit fidelity, not with the word length | Kanerva (1992), [LIT-921](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-921.md), §§3.5–3.7, read in full in [NOTE-779](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-779.md), after Jaeckel (1989a). An approximate derivation for uniform random data and exact retrieval cues. It does not cover noisy cues, which lower capacity, or clustered data, which the uniform design handles badly, and it does not contain the critical-distance analysis that is sometimes attributed to it. | Active |
| [THEORY-361](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-361.md) | When every object but one has full grade in exactly one of two attribute-sorted lists and the one has full grade in both, finding it under min takes at least about half the objects' worth of accesses for any algorithm that only reads the lists from the top and looks up objects already seen, and, with the tied objects in random order, about as many in expectation even for algorithms that may look up any object; a query on one attribute alone costs k accesses whatever the number of objects | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md): Example 6.3 and Theorem 6.4, the paper's proof that no algorithm is instance optimal once lucky lookups are allowed. With 2n + 1 objects, n + 1 high in each list and only one high in both, an algorithm that cannot guess must read at least n + 1 entries before it sees the target, and on a randomized family any deterministic algorithm needs at least n + 1 accesses in expectation. The paper uses the case to bound instance optimality. That it explains linear conjunction-search slopes in human vision is the record's analogy, not the paper's claim. | Active |
| [THEORY-363](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-363.md) | For finding the top k objects under a monotone combining function from m lists each sorted by one attribute, with sorted and random accesses the only costs, the threshold algorithm is correct and on every database costs at most a constant times what any correct algorithm that makes no wild guesses costs; the constant is m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, no deterministic algorithm does better when the function is strict, and once wild guesses are allowed no algorithm has such a guarantee on databases with ties | Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001; full version read as arXiv cs/0204046v1), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md). The threshold algorithm reads m attribute-sorted lists in parallel, looks up each new object's other grades, and stops when k seen objects score at least the combined score of the last grades read. For every monotone combining function it is instance optimal among correct algorithms that make no wild guesses (Theorem 6.1), with ratio m + m(m−1)c_R/c_S, tight for strict functions (Corollary 6.2, Theorem 9.1). It is a guarantee relative to a class of algorithms under an access-cost model. It does not say that top-k queries are cheap: the absolute cost depends on the data, and is linear in N for some conjunctive queries. | Active |
| [THEORY-365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-365.md) v3 | In one study of a stack of proximity graphs on nested random subsets of the data, each element's top layer drawn geometrically, greedy search on uniform random data in 8 dimensions needed a number of distance computations that grew no worse than logarithmically with the number of items and stayed below a single-layer navigable graph's at every size tested, and in 4 dimensions the beam width needed for a fixed recall saturated; the logarithmic bound is derived only for exact Delaunay graphs of bounded degree, which the index does not build, and on 200 million SIFT vectors the measured growth departs from it | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md) from arXiv v4. They build an index like a skip list, with proximity graphs in place of linked lists, and argue that search costs a constant per layer over O(log N) layers. That holds if each layer is an exact Delaunay graph of bounded mean degree. HNSW does not build such graphs, and Delaunay degree grows exponentially with dimension. For the graphs it does build, cost no worse than logarithmic is measured on uniform random data at d = 8, a saturating beam width at d = 4, and at d = 128 (200M SIFT) the growth departs from a logarithm. A proof for the graphs HNSW builds is QUESTION-187. The paper gives no worst-case bound and no recall guarantee. Construction is argued to cost about N searches. | Active |
| [THEORY-366](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-366.md) | With a fixed number of data points and a query drawn independently of them, if the variance of the p-th power of the query-to-point distance divided by its mean tends to zero, the farthest point comes within any factor 1 + ε of the nearest with probability tending to one; independent coordinates meet this condition, while data on a low-dimensional subspace, or queries that fall inside well-separated clusters, escape it | Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft (1999), [LIT-1099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1099.md), read in [NOTE-917](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-917.md) from the authors' 1998 technical report. Theorem 1: for n fixed data points and an independent query, var(d^p / E[d^p]) → 0 implies P[DMAX ≤ (1+ε)DMIN] → 1 for every ε > 0. The index m is arbitrary, so dimension enters only through the workload's distance distributions. IID coordinates and several correlated or non-identical workloads satisfy the condition; a diagonal line, two latent degrees of freedom and queries inside clusters do not. The condition is sufficient, not necessary. The result concerns the ratio of distances at fixed n, and does not show that real high-dimensional data loses contrast, or that indexes fail. | Active |
| [THEORY-368](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-368.md) v2 | On two-dimensional point sets constructed for the purpose, the authors' code for fast-preprocessing DiskANN, HNSW and NSG, at parameters from the original papers, in most cases found none or few of a query's five nearest neighbours until the search queue held about 10% of the points, for n from 10⁵ to 2·10⁶, and at that queue length ten graph indexes averaged recall@5 between 0.0 and 0.42; this is shown by experiment on one query per instance, and no theorem bounds these algorithms | Indyk and Xu (2023), [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md), read in [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md). | [THEORY-369](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-369.md) v2 | Under uniformly distributed, independent data and queries in the unit cube with Euclidean distance and a fixed number of points, an optimal nearest-neighbour search over any index that partitions points into blocks or convex clusters of at least two points must read a fraction of blocks that grows toward all of them as dimension rises; with a five-fold sequential advantage for scanning, estimates put the crossover at about 15–26 dimensions for rectangular and spherical bounding regions, and two tree indexes measured on 50,000 points lost to a scan beyond about 10 | Weber, Schek and Blott (1998), [LIT-1107](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1107.md), read in [NOTE-919](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-919.md). Under uniformity and independence, with the expected nearest-neighbour distance used as every query's radius and integrals evaluated by Monte Carlo, the fraction of blocks read passes the 20% line at about d = 15–20 for rectangular regions and 26 for spherical ones. A crude bound for any convex clustering puts it below 610. The often-quoted "around 10" is the measured crossover for an R*-tree and an X-tree. The VA-file, a scan of compact per-vector approximations, is the paper's alternative. Nothing is shown for data of low intrinsic dimension, and the finite-dimensional bounds are not rigorous as stated. The asymptotic statement, at fixed N and for clusters of two or more points, is proved by the record by a concentration argument. | Active |
| [THEORY-370](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-370.md) | On an n × n lattice whose nodes also get long-range links drawn with probability proportional to lattice distance to the power −r, a searcher that knows only the target's position and the links of nodes already reached delivers in expected time polylogarithmic in n only at r = 2: greedy routing then takes O((log n)²) steps, while for 0 ≤ r < 2 every such searcher needs Ω(n^((2−r)/3)) steps and for r > 2 Ω(n^((r−2)/(r−1))), even at r = 0 where short paths exist | Kleinberg (2000), [LIT-1103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1103.md), read in [NOTE-923](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-923.md). Proved for the two-dimensional lattice: with nodes, local links and the number of long-range links fixed, changing only the exponent r of the long-range link distribution moves the expected delivery time of the best decentralized searcher from O((log n)²) at r = 2 to a power of n at every other r, including r = 0, where paths of polylogarithmic length exist. The upper bound is proved only for one local and one long-range link per node; the k-dimensional statement (r = k) is asserted, not proved; the family is inverse power laws of a distance every node can compute, so it does not show that no other link structure is navigable. | Active |
| [THEORY-372](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-372.md) | For c-approximate near-neighbour search over n points in Euclidean space, space n^{1+ρu+o(1)} and query time n^{ρq+o(1)} are achievable on any data set whenever c²√ρq + (c²−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c²−1) (c√ρq + (c−1)√ρu ≥ √(2c−1) in Hamming space), and no list-of-points structure, the model of known data-independent hashing, does better on random instances; without that model the curve is matched only at query time n^{o(1)} by one or two cell probes | Andoni, Laarhoven, Razenshteyn and Waingarten (2017), [LIT-1120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1120.md), read in [NOTE-918](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-918.md) from the arXiv full version. A data-dependent tree of spherical caps, with different thresholds for filing points and for routing queries, realizes every pair of exponents on the curve, for worst-case data, with constant success probability; the equal-threshold point is LSH. On random instances with d = ω(log n), list-of-points structures cannot beat the curve (a lower bound the paper calls conditional), and one- or two-probe cell-probe structures need n^{(c/(c−1))²−o(1)} words, the curve's space at ρq = 0. Optimality for data-dependent schemes, for more probes, and for d = Θ(log n) is not shown. The curve prices space against per-query time for one query at a time; it has no workload and no build cost beyond space. | Active |
| [THEORY-376](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-376.md) v2 | In a simulated single-client, read-only database answering selection queries on one relation, describing cached data by the predicates of past queries let each query be answered partly from cache, with only the remainder Q ∧ ¬V sent to the server; this matched page caching on a clustered index, beat it on an unclustered one, and, on an unindexed attribute with a disk cache, answered over 60% of 1% queries without contacting the server; the cost of computing probe and remainder queries was not charged | Dar, Franklin, Jónsson, Srivastava and Tan (1996), [LIT-1113](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1113.md), read in [NOTE-904](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-904.md). In one simulator (one client, one server, a 10,000-tuple relation, 90% of queries in a hot 10%), semantic caching performed about like page caching on a clustered index, far better on an unclustered one, and on an unindexed attribute answered over 60% of 1% queries with no server scan. Space overhead depended on coalescing: 55 regions and about 275 factors for 1% queries without it. The result is measured, not proved; updates, joins and the CPU cost of reasoning about the cache's contents were left out, so it does not show that predicate-described storage pays when finding the reusable part is costly. | Active |
| [THEORY-379](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-379.md) v2 | Fagin's Algorithm finds the top k of N objects held in m attribute-sorted lists under any monotone combining function, and when the lists' orderings are independent with at least m − 1 of them uniformly random it does so with O(N^((m−1)/m) k^(1/m)) sorted and random accesses with arbitrarily high probability; with dependent orderings the bound can fail | Fagin (1996/1999), [LIT-1108](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1108.md), as reported by Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md). Fagin's own paper could not be obtained, and the reporting paper declines to describe the probability model ("off track"). It does correct one misreading: the only probabilistic assumption is independence of the lists' orderings, not a uniform distribution of grades. For two lists the bound is √(Nk). It does not hold for anti-correlated attributes, where any algorithm can need about half the objects. | Active |
| [THEORY-384](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-384.md) | A nearest-neighbour graph built by pruning each point's links against all other points with a factor α > 1, so that from every point some link is α times closer to any other point, lets greedy search from any start reach a ((α+1)/(α−1) + ε)-approximate nearest neighbour in O(log_α(∆/((α−1)ε))) steps of cost O((4α)^d log ∆), for doubling dimension d and aspect ratio ∆; the ratio is tight and the dependence on ∆ cannot be replaced by one on n, and the build takes O(n³) time done naively | Indyk and Xu (2023), [LIT-1112](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1112.md), read in [NOTE-910](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-910.md). Proved for DiskANN's "slow preprocessing" build, not the build DiskANN implements. The guarantee rests on one property of the graph (α-shortcut reachability, α > 1), gives a constant approximation, not exact search, is logarithmic in the aspect ratio ∆, which can exceed n by far, and has a per-step cost exponential in the doubling dimension. HNSW and NSG prune with α = 1 and are not covered. | Active |
| [THEORY-385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-385.md) v2 | In HNSW over 10-dimensional data in 100 isolated clusters, linking each new item to its nearest neighbours leaves part of the bottom layer unreachable from the entry point and caps recall well short of 1 however wide the query search, while linking a candidate only when it is nearer the new item than to any neighbour already kept keeps that layer connected and reaches recall near 1 with about half the links; on uniform data at 10 and 64 dimensions the two rules differ little; shown in Malkov and Yashunin's own tests on 10 million points and in an independent re-run on 30,000, which found the nearest-neighbour rule capped at a recall@10 of 0.72 to 0.83 against 0.999, at matched build cost too | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md). In HNSW, each new element's neighbours are chosen either as its M nearest candidates or by a pruning rule that keeps a candidate only if it is nearer the new element than to any neighbour already kept, a rule related to the relative neighbourhood graph. On 10M random d = 10 vectors in 100 isolated clusters, nearest-neighbour links failed to reach high recall and the pruning rule did not. In every test reported, the rule was at least as good. Its gain was largest at low dimension, at high recall, and on clustered data, and small on uniform or very high-dimensional data. These are the authors' benchmarks: one clustered dataset, synthetic, with no independent replication in this reading. Re-run independently at smaller scale on promotion (2026-10-20), with the same result. | Active |
| [THEORY-388](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-388.md) | Locality-sensitive hashing answers approximate near-neighbour queries over n points with O(n^ρ) hash evaluations in O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space, where ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2) is set by how much more often near pairs collide than far ones and is at most 1/(1+ε) for approximation 1+ε in Hamming space, with constant success probability per query; the paper gives upper bounds only and proves no limit on what organizing can buy | Indyk and Motwani (1998), [LIT-1106](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1106.md), read in [NOTE-905](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-905.md) from the authors' 1999 expanded version, compared with the STOC text. A hash family under which points within r1 collide with probability at least p1 and points beyond r2 with at most p2 gives n^ρ random tables, each storing every point: O(dn + n^{1+ρ}) space and O(n^ρ) hash evaluations per query, ρ = ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2), for the decision version, which ring-cover trees connect to approximate nearest neighbour with polylog overhead. Bit sampling gives ρ ≤ 1/(1+ε) in Hamming space and, by embedding, ℓ_p for p in [1, 2]; the STOC text states 1/ε and only for ε > 1. Grid bucketing gives Õ(d) queries for n·O(1/ε)^d preprocessing. Preprocessing is counted as space. Nothing is proved about whether these exponents can be beaten. | Active |
| [THEORY-480](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-480.md) | Where a general-search monopoly was kept by exclusive distribution deals, the court in United States v. Google treated the user-interaction data that scale produced as the fruit to be remedied, and held that sharing the raw data and index metadata, but not the engineered signals and models built from them, can restore rivals' ability to compete without breaking the firm up; that the sharing will work is the court's expectation, not a finding | Mehta (2025), [LIT-006](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-006.md), the remedies opinion, read in full in [NOTE-004](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-004.md). The court finds that exclusive distribution produced a scale advantage (9× the queries of all rivals; 93% of unique phrases seen only by Google), calls it a fruit of the violation, and remedies it with raw data and syndication rather than with divestiture, on a sliding scale of causal connection. The opinion also finds no proof that search scale gives Google's GenAI a quality edge (op. p. 156), which is an absence of proof, not a finding that there is none. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-697](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-697.md) | Sparse distributed memory's read weights each stored pattern by the number of hard locations within the read radius of both query and pattern, a ball-intersection count that falls roughly exponentially in Hamming distance over a local window, so softmax attention over cosine similarity of unit-norm queries and keys, with a fitted inverse temperature, approximates the SDM read there; the approximation cannot hold globally, since the binary count vanishes beyond twice the radius, and its inverse temperature comes from a regression, not from the paper's analytic bound | Bricken & Pehlevan (2021), [LIT-269](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-269.md), read in full in [NOTE-242](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-242.md), which re-evaluated the intersection formula and the fit. The exact intersection (Eq. 2) is checked against Kanerva's lune formula and simulation; eight SDM and fitted-softmax variants retrieve almost identically on random patterns, MNIST and CIFAR-10, with three named exceptions. The intersection is a staircase in distance, the fit holds to about dv = 20 for d = 15, the analytic β of App. B.2 is about 2–2.5 times too small, and every optimal radius assumes random patterns and addresses. The GPT-2 "confirmation" and the cerebellar implementation of attention are argument, not demonstration. | Active |
| [THEORY-815](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-815.md) | Layering a navigable small-world graph on nested random subsets of the data, with links separated by length scale and each layer's degree capped, makes greedy nearest-neighbour search cost grow logarithmically with the number of items on data of low intrinsic dimension, where the single-layer graph's cost grows polylogarithmically | Malkov and Yashunin (2020), [LIT-1098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1098.md), read in [NOTE-916](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-916.md), argue that HNSW's hierarchy is what makes greedy search logarithmic: constant cost per layer over O(log N) layers, against the polylogarithmic cost of their earlier flat graph. | [THEORY-832](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-832.md) | For strict combining functions and m attribute-sorted lists of N objects whose orderings are probabilistically independent, no correct top-k algorithm does essentially better than Fagin's Algorithm in the worst case with high probability: every one needs on the order of N^((m−1)/m) k^(1/m) accesses | Fagin (1996/1999), [LIT-1108](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1108.md), as reported by Fagin, Lotem and Naor (2001), [LIT-1115](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1115.md), Sections 1 and 3, read in [NOTE-924](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-924.md): "his algorithm is optimal with high probability in the worst case if the aggregation function is strict ... and if the orderings in the sorted lists are probabilistically independent."
